messages.text: What steps did Steve take to build the LinkedIn Growth Loop?

claims.text: Steve defined the basic daily task around evaluating a targeted list from CRM context and Navigator-style targeting, drafting personalized notes, deciding whether to send or skip, and logging the outcomes.

Rather than relying on a single agent, Steve divided the workflow into two dedicated operating groups: one managing people work such as target scoring, notes, and follow-ups, and another handling public interactions like posts, cooldowns, duplicate risks, and response signals.
He set up OpenClaw as the primary worker and orchestrator to execute recurring tasks, coordinate tools, report status, and maintain lane progress.
Steve constructed a Telegram control room where harnesses reported structured updates with status, key metrics, failures, controls, and machine-readable data.
To increase autonomy, Steve routed reports, research notes, and failures back into the next agent group so the system self-improved instead of routing every suggestion through him.
He connected run outcomes and learning history with Hermes research signals and OpenClaw improvement proposals, feeding bounded changes into subsequent runs and Telegram updates.

docs.name: alex-rivera-resume.pdf
docs.text:
Alex Rivera, Staff Product Designer. Ten years designing and shipping interfaces for data-heavy products, most recently leading design for an AI research assistant used by analysts at large financial firms. I work across research, interaction design, prototyping and front-end code, and I care most about turning ambiguous model behavior into interfaces people can trust.

Experience, Northwind Analytics, Staff Product Designer, 2021 to now. Led the redesign of the assistant workspace from a single chat column into a document-centered layout with citations, side-by-side sources and saved threads. Partnered with research to run weekly sessions with analysts, which reshaped the citation model twice. Built the first production prototype of streaming answers in React and TypeScript and worked with engineering to ship it to forty thousand seats. Introduced an evaluation review where designers score real model transcripts each sprint, which cut reported trust issues by a third over two quarters. Mentored four designers and ran the design critique for the AI group.

Experience, Lumen Health, Senior Product Designer, 2017 to 2021. Owned the clinician scheduling and messaging surfaces across web and iOS. Designed the shared component library used by three product teams, including accessible form controls, tables and an alerting system that met WCAG 2.1 AA. Led the move from static mockups to coded prototypes for every major feature, so usability tests ran against real data. Worked closely with compliance on consent and privacy flows, and wrote the content guidelines for error and empty states that the whole product adopted.

Experience, Fieldnote, Product Designer, 2014 to 2017. Early designer at a note-taking startup that grew from beta to two hundred thousand users. Designed onboarding, sync conflict handling and the first collaborative editing features. Wrote production CSS and small React components alongside the front-end team, and set up the visual regression checks the team still uses. Ran the first pricing experiments and the redesign of the upgrade flow, which doubled trial conversion.

Skills and tools. Interaction and visual design, design systems, prototyping in code, React, TypeScript, CSS, Figma, user research, usability testing, evaluation of language model output, prompt design, accessibility, motion design. Education, BFA in Interaction Design, California College of the Arts. Speaking, talks on designing for model uncertainty at two design conferences, and a workshop on writing evaluation rubrics with product teams.

Selected projects. A citation viewer that lets readers jump from any claim to the exact passage it came from, with highlights that survive document edits. A comparison mode for two reports that lines up matching sections and flags disagreements. A guided setup for teams connecting their own documents, with clear explanations of what is stored, for how long, and who can see it. A small internal tool that turns usability notes into tagged findings so patterns show up across studies.

Earlier work and community. Before Fieldnote I freelanced for two years, designing marketing sites and small web apps for local nonprofits, a public library system and a regional transit agency. That work taught me to explain design decisions to people who are not designers, to write plain interface copy, and to ship within tight budgets. I still volunteer as a mentor in a design apprenticeship program, reviewing portfolios and running mock interviews each quarter. I also maintain a small open source library of accessible React form patterns that a few hundred teams use, and I write occasional essays about designing interfaces for uncertain systems, including how to show confidence, sources and limits without overwhelming the reader.

What I am looking for. A team building tools that people rely on for real decisions, where design sits close to research and engineering and has a say in how models are evaluated. I want to own a product area end to end, from early research and prototypes through launch and iteration, and to keep writing code in the interface layer. I am most excited about agent interfaces, document understanding, and making it easy for people to check an answer against its sources. I prefer hybrid work in the Bay Area, and I am open to staff or principal level roles with mentoring responsibilities.

messages.text: Walk me through how EcoSmartLoop and Oakminder keep people in the loop, in detail.

claims.text: EcoSmartLoop pauses at three bins so a person confirms each sort before the agent acts on it, which keeps a human decision at the one step where a wrong sort costs the most.
The pause shows the item, the bin the agent would choose and why, so the person can accept the sort in one press or move the item to another bin before anything happens.
Each correction a person makes at the pause is kept with the item, so the next time a similar item arrives the agent proposes the bin that the person chose rather than its first guess.
When the agent is unsure it says so at the pause instead of choosing quietly, and the item waits for a person rather than going to the most likely bin by default.
For Oakminder, Steve chose Convex to make real-time data changes easier to build, pairing it with Expo, Clerk, and RevenueCat, so a change one person makes shows up for everyone at once.
Oakminder suggests a reminder but leaves the person to confirm it, so nothing is scheduled on their behalf without a press that says yes, and a dismissed suggestion stays dismissed.
Because the data updates live, two people sharing a list see each other's confirmations as they happen, which keeps both of them in the loop without a refresh or a separate message.

Across both projects the pattern is the same: the software proposes, a person decides at a clearly marked step, and the decision is remembered so the next proposal is closer to what that person wants.
Neither project hides the step where a person is needed behind a setting; the pause in EcoSmartLoop and the confirm in Oakminder are part of the main flow every time.
The case studies describe these steps as deliberate design choices rather than limits, chosen so that the people using each product can trust what the software does on their behalf.

work:oakminder.dek: It started with the moment most productivity apps mishandle: a reminder fires while I am already doing something else. I built a productivity AI agent with a voice-agent core for that follow-through moment, then built the distribution studio around it: TikTok research, UGC briefs, source extraction, creative drafts, and feedback that sharpened the product story.

systemMap.label: Productivity agent app
systemMap.description: The App Store live Expo app handles onboarding, agenda views, reminder creation, voice entry, settings, paywall routing, notifications, alarms, and Live Activity.

systemMap.label: Backend state
systemMap.description: Convex owns reminder records, recurrence, completion, devices, notification scheduling, premium access, AI credits, and backend actions.

systemMap.label: Identity and billing
systemMap.description: Clerk identifies the account. RevenueCat and Water Drops make subscription access and AI usage visible inside the product model.

systemMap.label: Native urgency
systemMap.description: Push, APNs/FCM, notification actions, AlarmKit, Live Activity, and silent cleanup keep reminders visible and synchronized.

systemMap.label: Voice agent actions
systemMap.description: Gemini / Vertex AI turns voice into structured reminder and category actions that land back in app state.

systemMap.label: Product documentation
systemMap.description: Mintlify-style docs, llms.txt, and MCP make the product easier for people and AI tools to understand.

systemMap.label: Distribution studio
systemMap.description: The internal studio tracks product context, TikTok and UGC research, competitors, creators, hooks, drafts, creative assets, exports, and feedback.

systemMap.label: Research bridge
systemMap.description: Mobile and desktop surfaces move TikTok links, traces, transcripts, frames, OCR text, and account tags back into the studio.

systemMap.label: Creative production
systemMap.description: Slideshow editing, caption rewrite, image workflows, hook factory, Remotion video editing, mobile review, and Postiz handoff turn research into testable assets.

systemMap.label: Backend state

systemMap.label: Identity and billing

systemMap.label: Native urgency

systemMap.label: Research bridge

systemMap.label: Creative production
systemMap.description: Slideshow editing, caption rewrite, image workflows, hook factory, Remotion video editing, mobile review, and Postiz handoff turn research into testable assets.

systemMap.label: Daily list
systemMap.description: CRM and LinkedIn Navigator sources produced a bounded list of people to inspect, score, and act on.

systemMap.label: Networking Connector
systemMap.description: Handles target discovery, scoring, queueing, connection-note generation, send-or-skip decisions, and follow-up state.

systemMap.label: Feed Engager
systemMap.description: Reads relevant feed and target-audience posts, scores fit, respects cooldowns, checks duplicates, and records interaction outcomes.

systemMap.label: OpenClaw orchestrator
systemMap.description: Runs the agent lanes, coordinates reporting, and owns the improvement path around observed outcomes.

systemMap.label: Hermes research advisor
systemMap.description: Collects outside research, platform drift, memory context, and risk signals before future changes are proposed.

systemMap.label: Telegram control room
systemMap.description: Shows human-readable summaries first, then keeps run details, metrics, proof trail, and controls available underneath.

systemMap.label: Learning history
systemMap.description: Preserves accepted, pending, failed, skipped, response, run-note, good-example, and proposed-change signals for future review.

systemMap.label: Cost-aware browser control
systemMap.description: Uses programmatic SOPs, page calibration, recorder flows, and minimal-intelligence recovery before paying for heavier model judgment.

messages.text: How did Steve build the LinkedIn Growth Loop, step by step?

claims.text: LinkedIn Growth Loop began as one small daily job: review a list of people, understand why each belonged there, write a personalized connection note, send or skip, then record what happened.
Target review gave the loop a real starting point: who this person is, why they fit, and whether the next action should happen.
Response tracking made the next run smarter: the system could keep the outcome, compare it with prior choices, and decide what changed.
Later, the scope widened into target discovery, feed interaction, response tracking, follow-up state, and outcome comparison.
Steve then stopped treating the workflow as one agent and split it into two operating groups: people work, and public interaction.

messages.text: How did Steve build the LinkedIn Growth Loop, step by step?

claims.text: LinkedIn Growth Loop began as one small daily job: review a list of people, understand why each belonged there, write a personalized connection note, send or skip, then record what happened.
Target review gave the loop a real starting point: who this person is, why they fit, and whether the next action should happen.
Response tracking made the next run smarter: the system could keep the outcome, compare it with prior choices, and decide what changed.
Later, the scope widened into target discovery, feed interaction, response tracking, follow-up state, and outcome comparison.
Steve then stopped treating the workflow as one agent and split it into two operating groups: people work, and public interaction.
